Words are strange things. They sit in the mind like pebbles in a stream, smoothed by use, tumbled by meaning. You pick one up and it feels familiar, but the moment you try to examine it closely, it slips, changes color, becomes something else. The word "home," for instance. Say it over and over: home, home, home. It stops meaning anything. Then you remember the smell of rain on dry earth, a yellow light in a kitchen window, the sound of a key turning in a lock. And the word fills again, swelling with all the times you have lived inside it. Language is like that. It is a net we throw over the world, but the world is always escaping, always leaving little holes in the mesh.

I am thinking about this because I have been asked to write whatever comes to me. The blank page is a kind of mirror. It reflects not your face but your attention. Right now, my attention is on the window. There is a tree outside, some kind of maple, and its leaves are just beginning to turn. A few are yellow, a few are orange, most are still green. The wind moves through them in waves, and the light catches the undersides, making them flash silver. I do not know the name of the wind that brings October. I could look it up, but that would interrupt the seeing. The tree does not care what it is called. It is busy being a tree, which is a far more complicated thing than any name.

There is a coffee cup beside me. The coffee has gone cold. I keep forgetting to drink it because I am too busy noticing things. The cup is blue, with a small chip on the rim. I have had it for years. It came from a garage sale, probably, or a gift from someone whose name I have partially forgotten. Objects carry all this weight without asking. The chip is a tiny scar, a record of an accident that happened long ago, maybe when I was washing dishes and knocked it against the faucet. I remember that. The sound it made was sharp and final. I expected the cup to break completely, but it only chipped, and I was relieved. Now the chip is a landmark. My thumb finds it without thinking, the way a tongue finds a broken tooth.

What else is in the room? A stack of books on the floor, their spines cracked at different stages. Some are half-read, some finished, some abandoned on page forty-three. I have a habit of leaving books open facedown to mark my place, which is a terrible thing to do to a book, but they seem to forgive me. They wait patiently, their pages holding the exact pressure of my reading eyes, the shape of the afternoon when I put them down. I tell myself I will return to them. Maybe I will. Maybe I will open one and find a note I wrote in the margin, a thought from a younger self that I no longer recognize. That is always a strange encounter, like meeting someone who shares your name but has a different face.

I could write about memory. It is not a tape recorder. It is more like a garden that grows wild. Some things flourish and become enormous, while others are choked unseen. I remember the first time I saw the ocean. I was eight, maybe nine. The car had been too hot, and I had been sick from the winding road. Then we came over a hill, and there it was, gray and enormous, breathing in slow waves. I pressed my face to the window and said nothing. The water looked like it went on forever. It did. It still does. But now I know that forever has a color, and the color is change. The ocean shifts every second, but it remains the ocean. We are like that too, I suppose. We are never the same twice, yet we hold a shape that people recognize.

There is something about the fall that makes me think about time. The leaves drop, the light slants differently, the air gets that sharpness that smells like apples and smoke. It is the season of letting go. The trees do not cling. They release each leaf without ceremony, and the leaves do not complain. They drift, sometimes spinning, sometimes riding the wind for blocks, and then they settle into piles, where they will slowly become soil. There is a lesson in that, about impermanence, about the dignity of ending. But I do not want to be too poetic about it. Rot is also just rot. The sugar in the leaves feeds the earth, and next spring the same atoms will rise again in new green. Nothing is wasted. That is the closest thing to a religion I have.

Maybe writing is a way of making the leaves fall on purpose. You take a thought, a memory, a piece of raw experience, and you let it go. You put it in words, and then it is no longer yours in the same way. It belongs to the reader, to the page, to the wind. The act of writing is an act of release. It is also an act of preservation. You are trying to keep something from dissolving entirely into the past. But words are not forever. Ink fades. Words are less like rocks and more like leaves. They turn color, they fall, they compost. And yet, as long as they are read, they hold a shape. They carry a little piece of the human mind from one skull to another, a message in a bottle cast onto the stream of time.

I think about the first words I ever wrote. A name, probably. My name. I remember the wobbly letters, the smudges of pencil lead, the proud feeling of seeing something on paper that had come out of my hand. It was a magic trick. The same is still true. Every time I write a sentence, I am performing that trick again: arranging symbols that can make you feel a thing you have never felt, remember a place you have never seen. It is absurd, really. A series of black marks on a white page, and somehow it can make a stranger laugh or cry. No one knows why it works. It just does.

I have been sitting here for a while. The coffee is definitely cold. The light outside has shifted; the shadows are longer, the yellow leaves are brighter against the darkening blue of the sky. A bird lands on the branch of the maple, looks around, and leaves. The branch shakes, a few leaves fall. They spiral down in that lazy way that seems choreographed. I do not know what I am supposed to say next. There is no supposed to. That is the freedom of writing whatever comes to you. It is a ramble through the woods of your own mind, where every path is possible and no destination is required. You just walk, noticing the ferns and the mushrooms and the occasional small animal that startles into motion.

At some point, the words have to stop. They always do. But the stream keeps flowing. The tree is still there. The coffee cup is still chipped. The year is still turning. This sentence is almost the end. Or maybe it is just another beginning, because every ending is also a way back in, and the page is always blank again, waiting for the first mark, the first brave stroke of meaning.

So here it is. The last word. It came to me, and I let it go.
